historical_timeline.summary: Born Benjamin Leiner in New York City to Orthodox Jewish immigrants from Russia.
Begins fighting professionally as Benny Leonard, keeping it from his parents.
Wins the world lightweight championship from Freddie Welsh.
Retires as undefeated lightweight champion, at his mother's wish, wealthy and unmarked.
Loses most of his savings in the stock market crash.
Comes back as a welterweight at 35; knocked out by Jimmy McLarnin in October 1932 and retires for good.
Serving in the U.S. Maritime Service; returns to boxing as a referee in New York and teaches boxing at City College.
Collapses and dies in the ring at St. Nicholas Arena while refereeing, at 51; the cause is given as a heart attack in most sources and a cerebral hemorrhage in one.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Hypertensive heart disease and sudden cardiac death risk in a man whose job is physical: a 50-year-old professional boxing referee and boxing instructor, a former champion who lost his savings years ago and works to rebuild them, is found at his license examination to have stage 2 hypertension, with breathlessness and chest tightness late in long nights in hot arenas and left ventricular hypertrophy on the ECG. The episode covers the evaluation of exertional symptoms with exercise stress echocardiography under the 1941 AHA/ACC chest pain guideline; telling hypertensive hypertrophy from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and athlete's heart; sudden cardiac death risk in left ventricular hypertrophy; a coronary calcium score that changes the statin decision under the 1946 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline and the 1943 chronic coronary disease guideline; a two-drug single-pill start, home blood pressure monitoring, laboratory checks after each change and a target below 130/80 mmHg under the 1945 AHA/ACC blood pressure guideline; volume depletion on a thiazide in summer heat, sick-day rules and a change to a calcium channel blocker; aspirin by shared decision; a return-to-work plan for refereeing, with heat, hydration, warning symptoms and defibrillators at the venue; and financial strain and worry as social factors in care, with low-cost generic once-daily medicines.

assessment.assessment: Not ischemic. An exercise stress echocardiogram was chosen because it tests for ischemia, measures his working capacity and shows the blood pressure response to effort; it showed no inducible ischemia at about 10.5 METs. The symptoms are best explained by a steep rise in blood pressure on exertion (to 226/98 mmHg) in a thickened, stiff ventricle, made worse by heat; they should settle as blood pressure is controlled

Hypertensive heart disease. The hypertrophy is concentric and modest (septum 13 mm, septal-to-posterior ratio 1.1) with no systolic anterior motion, no outflow gradient, a normal-sized cavity and diastolic dysfunction, in a man with stage 2 hypertension; this fits hypertension and not hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and an athlete's heart is unlikely at 50 years and years after competitive training. If the hypertrophy does not regress after six to twelve months of good control, or a family history emerges, cardiac MRI would be the next test

Left ventricular hypertrophy raises the risk of sudden cardiac death, and controlling blood pressure lowers it as the hypertrophy regresses. He has no fainting, palpitations or arrhythmia on exercise, a normal ejection fraction and a normal QTc, so ambulatory ECG monitoring and an implantable defibrillator are not indicated; monitoring would be needed for palpitations or fainting. Potassium should be kept in the normal range on the diuretic. He should know the warning symptoms, and the venues where he works should have a defibrillator at ringside and staff trained in CPR

A coronary calcium score of 186, above 100 and about the 80th percentile, shows coronary atherosclerosis and favors a statin: atorvastatin 40 mg, aiming for LDL below 70 mg/dL and a fall of at least 50%, with a lipid panel at eight to twelve weeks. Low-dose aspirin may be considered with a score over 100, but not while blood pressure is uncontrolled because of the bleeding risk; it should be revisited as a shared decision once blood pressure is at goal. Routine repeat stress testing is not recommended without new symptoms
